claims.text: For COVID-19 in London, an SLIR model with homogeneous mixing and a flat IFR achieved an age-fairness score of F(age) = 0.577 [0.569, 0.584].
For COVID-19 in London, an SLIR model with age-stratified contacts and a flat IFR achieved an age-fairness score of F(age) = 0.528 [0.521, 0.535].
For COVID-19 in London, an SLIR model combining age-stratified contacts with an age-dependent IFR achieved a fairness score of F(age) = 0.923 [0.919, 0.927].
For COVID-19 in London, an SLIR model combining homogeneous mixing with a heterogeneous IFR achieved a fairness score of F(age) = 0.976 [0.973, 0.979].
In New York City COVID-19 modeling, a baseline model with equal susceptibility and homogeneous mixing across racial/ethnic groups yielded a fairness score of F(race) = 0.714 [0.705, 0.724].
In New York City COVID-19 modeling, introducing variable susceptibility with homogeneous IFR increased racial/ethnic fairness to F(race) = 0.901 [0.889, 0.912].
In New York City COVID-19 modeling, a model with homogeneous IFR and assortative mixing achieved the highest racial/ethnic fairness of F(race) = 0.906 [0.893, 0.918].
In New York City COVID-19 models, a baseline model with equally distributed contact rates and heterogeneous IFR achieved a fairness score of F(race) = 0.621 [0.613, 0.630].

In Santiago COVID-19 simulations ranked by Human Development Index (HDI), integrating human mobility data yielded an average RCI fairness score of F(HDI) = 0.97 compared to 0.93 without mobility data.
In Santiago COVID-19 simulations treated as unordered comunas, including human mobility data increased the average Theil-based fairness score from 0.63 to 0.79.

In multidimensional agent-based models of New York City, an age-stratified random network achieved a geographic fairness score of F(geo) = 0.934 [0.868, 0.982], while an age-stratified hybrid network achieved F(geo) = 0.937 [0.868, 0.981].
A full Theil-index-based vaccine allocation strategy (gamma = 1) in NYC yielded an overall median death reduction of 73.9% [56.6, 97.9] compared to 68.2% [53.8, 94.2] for a population-based strategy.

Vaccine allocation based on death rates reduced overall mortality by 72.1% [55.3, 97.1] but decreased relative death reduction for the White majority group to 65.2% [45.7, 96.3] relative to the population-based baseline of 68.9% [54.3, 94.4].

Model fairness can be defined mathematically as an epidemic model's ability to capture the observed unequal distribution of disease burden according to equity-related demographic or socioeconomic traits.

evidence.description: "This model does not adequately capture the higher concentration of deaths in the elderly groups, as shown by its fairness score of F(age) = 0.577 [0.569, 0.584]."
"Similarly, the model considering a flat IFR and an age-stratified contact matrix has a fairness score of F(age) = 0.528 [0.521, 0.535]."
"The model considering both age-stratified contacts and an age-dependent IFR has a fairness score of F(age) = 0.923 [0.919, 0.927] (Fig. 1b purple dots)"
"...while the one combining homogeneous mixing with a heterogeneous IFR has an even higher score of F(age)=0.976 [0.973, 0.979] (Fig. 1b turquoise dots)."

"As expected, the baseline model generates an equally distributed number of deaths among racial and ethnic groups, thus failing to capture the observed inequalities. Its fairness score is F(race) = 0.714 [0.705, 0.724]."
"By introducing variable susceptibility and maintaining a homogeneous IFR for all groups, the fairness of the model increases to F(race) = 0.901 [0.889, 0.912]."
"A model with a homogeneous IFR and assortative mixing achieves the highest fairness F(race) = 0.906 [0.893, 0.918]."
"For instance, a baseline model with equally distributed contact rates and heterogeneous IFR only achieves F(race) = 0.621 [0.613, 0.630] (Table S7)."
"According to Eq. 2, the model with mobility is characterized by an average fairness score of F(HDI) = 0.97, while excluding mobility data decreases the score to 0.93."
"In this case, by including human mobility data, the average model’s fairness increases from 0.63 to 0.79."

"This is exemplified by the Theil-index fairness scores of the age-stratified random network model (F(geo)=0.934 [0.868, 0.982]) compared to the age-stratified hybrid network model (F(geo) = 0.937 [0.868, 0.981])."
"Table 1 compares the relative reduction in deaths achieved by different vaccine allocation strategies... Population-based 68.2 [53.8, 94.2]... Theil-index-based 73.9 [56.6, 97.9]"

"However, allocating vaccines according to group-specific death risk increases overall mortality reduction (72.1%) mainly in minority groups (Hispanic, Black, and Asian), while the majority group (Whites) experiences an increase in mortality relative to the population-based baseline." (Table 1: White death reduction 65.2% vs 68.9%).
"We define the fairness of an epidemic model as its ability to capture the (un)equal distribution of disease burden according to one or more equity-related features."

methodologies.name: Relative Concentration Index (RCI) Model Fairness Metric
methodologies.description: Quantifies model fairness for ordered social groups by taking 1 minus the absolute difference between model and empirical Relative Concentration Indices divided by 2.
datasets: London weekly COVID-19 mortality data by age
conditions: Ordered demographic/socioeconomic groups along a hierarchical continuum

methodologies.name: Theil Index Component-based Model Fairness Metric
methodologies.description: Evaluates model fairness for unordered social groups or regions using an exponential of the negative sum of absolute differences between model and observed group-level Theil index components.
conditions: Unordered categorical subgroups (e.g., race, ethnicity, or unranked spatial units)

methodologies.name: Theil-index-weighted Vaccine Allocation Strategy
methodologies.description: Distributes vaccine doses across subgroups by weighting each subgroup's population share by its empirical Theil index ill-health component via parameter gamma.
conditions: Simulated second epidemic wave with 20% sterilizing vaccine coverage

limitations.text: Computational epidemiology lacks standard frameworks and general transferable definitions to address inequalities and model fairness systematically across pathogens and contexts.

The framework did not address how to correctly identify from available data which equity-related variables to include or how to mechanistically link social causes with biological disease exposure mechanisms.

The vaccine allocation analysis relied on a stylized proof-of-concept scenario that assumed sterilizing immunity and omitted operational constraints, vaccine supply limits, adverse impacts, and waning immunity.
Covasim agent-based simulations in New York City could not explicitly represent inter-borough coupling because the simulator lacked spatial coupling functionality.
The framework was applied post-hoc to already calibrated models rather than directly integrating fairness scores into model fitting or policy optimization objective functions.

future_work.text: Integrate operational conditions such as logistics, vaccine hesitancy, and governance to evaluate fairness-informed allocation under real-world constraints.
Incorporate fairness metrics directly into model fitting or policy optimization routines as objective functions or constraints rather than evaluating post hoc.
Conduct more extensive evaluations of fairness metrics across broader epidemic types and varied intervention scenarios.
